items.original_title: Alkagesta takes ownership of eight bunker vessels with Energy Petrol deal

The deal marks Alkagesta’s first move into owning vessels, the company said. Along with the fleet, it brings a long-term lease on 28,000 cbm of storage tanks at a terminal in Gebze. Alkagesta says Energy Petrol ranks third among physical bunker suppliers in the port of Istanbul. Energy Petrol, founded in 1997, will keep trading under its own name. Alkagesta agreed to buy the company in October, and the share transfer is now complete. items.title: IMO Chief Calls for Strict Enforcement of SOLAS Rules in Strait of Hormuz
items.original_title: IMO Chief Calls for Strict Enforcement of SOLAS Rules in Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: FILE PHOTO: Oil/Chemical Tanker "Bald Man" at the Port of Fujairah, as the U.S.-Israel conflict with Iran limits marine traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, in Fujairah, United Arab Emirates, May 6, 2026. REUTERS/Amr Alfiky/File Photo International Maritime Organization (IMO) Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez has called on governments to step up enforcement of international maritime regulations in the Strait of Hormuz, warning that unsafe shipping practices are adding to the risks facing seafarers amid the ongoing conflict. In a statement issued Wednesday, Dominguez raised concerns about vessels transiting the strategic waterway without complying with basic international safety requirements, including provisions of the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea (SOLAS). The warning comes as commercial shipping continues to face attacks in and around the Strait of Hormuz, where the IMO has now verified more than 130 incidents involving merchant vessels since the conflict began on February 28. The IMO chief specifically cited reports of substandard vessels, ships concealing their IMO identification numbers, vessels operating under fraudulent registrations or false flags, and other unsafe practices. The latest appeal follows last week’s meeting of the IMO Council in London, where member states called for stronger protections for seafarers and reiterated that vital shipping lanes must remain open, safe and secure.

items.title: UK Launches ‘Atlantic Net’ to Track Russian Submarines and Protect Undersea Cables
items.original_title: UK Launches ‘Atlantic Net’ to Track Russian Submarines and Protect Undersea Cables
items.summary: The UK is moving ahead with a £90 million investment in autonomous underwater systems, advanced sensors and artificial intelligence to strengthen the Royal Navy’s ability to track Russian submarines and protect critical infrastructure in the North Atlantic. The initiative, known as Atlantic Net, is the first operational phase of the Royal Navy’s broader Atlantic Bastion programme, which aims to combine crewed warships and submarines with autonomous systems to improve underwater surveillance and counter potential threats to subsea communications cables, energy networks and shipping routes. The UK Ministry of Defence announced the investment Tuesday during the International Sea Power Conference in Oslo, Norway, alongside a framework agreement with UK-based marine robotics company Ocean Infinity Solutions. The system will combine underwater sensors, uncrewed platforms, communications technology and AI-powered data analysis to detect and track potentially hostile submarine activity. The programme is expected to become operational in 2027, according to UK Defence Minister Luke Pollard, who outlined the plans in a speech in Oslo. “This investment gives the Royal Navy new technology to find threats earlier and protect our critical infrastructure, while also backing British business.” The investment comes amid growing concern among European governments and NATO allies over the vulnerability of underwater infrastructure, particularly communications cables and energy connections that are essential to both civilian economies and military operations.

items.title: Ports could future-proof to beat box terminal congestion
items.original_title: Ports could future-proof to beat box terminal congestion
items.summary: In recent months, a daily review of container terminal utilisation levels has become something of a ‘must-read’ for supply chain planners seeking to understand where boxes may be delayed, and for how long. That remains an art rather than science, but indicates how the container shipping industry has experienced something of a paradigm shift into an era in which waves of mega-congestion ripple across the port and shipping system. Terminal occupancy levels – ie, how many containers are sitting in a yard awaiting either a truck or loading on a vessel – continue to sit way above what these facilities were designed to handle. Some of this is beyond terminal operators’ control – they have no say over when vessels arrive, or how delayed they might have been at the previous port; while wars, weather, and other disruptive events are in the hands of the gods – or people who think of themselves as such… However, in the spirit of supply chain resilience, they could be far better prepared to tackle congestion when it arises.

items.title: Monjasa seals biggest-ever fleet deal with five-tanker swoop
items.original_title: Monjasa seals biggest-ever fleet deal with five-tanker swoop
items.summary: Danish bunker supplier and shipowner Monjasa has acquired five sister product tankers from Germany’s Bernhard Schulte in its largest-ever fleet deal, strengthening its marine fuels operations in West Africa. The Fredericia-based group has picked up five 2010- and 2011-built tankers of around 16,500 dwt each. The purchase price has not been disclosed. Four vessels, renamed Monjasa Tracer, Monjasa Tuner, Monjasa Twister and Monjasa Tracker , have already joined the fleet and are trading in West Africa and Northwest Europe. The fifth, Monjasa Trigger , is set to follow by the end of November. The acquisition takes Monjasa’s owned fleet to 20 tankers, alongside around 10 ships on time charter. Group chief executive Anders Østergaard described the purchase as the company’s largest single tonnage acquisition, highlighting the benefits of taking on five identical vessels with established operating costs and technical requirements. “Finding five sister vessels of this quality, at competitive market terms and with an operating profile that fits our existing fleet, is not something you come across every day,” he said. The deal builds on Monjasa’s earlier tanker investments in West Africa, including the 2023 acquisition of the 68,589 dwt Monjasa Leader and the 13,051 dwt Monjasa Refiner , which were brought in for floating storage and bunker supply operations, respectively.

items.title: Coal’s new world order takes shape
items.original_title: Coal’s new world order takes shape
items.summary: Coal’s changing trade map is creating winners and losers across dry bulk shipping in 2026, with Indonesian exports retreating, southern African shipments setting records and Asian import demand increasingly fractured. Clarksons Research forecasts seaborne coal trade will edge up just 1% this year to 1.343bn tonnes. Beneath that modest increase, Indonesian exports are projected to fall 6% to 496.9m tonnes, while Australian shipments climb 4% to 371.3m tonnes. BIMCO reports coal imports dropped 7% in the first ten months despite coal-fired electricity generation rising around 9%. BRS says coal inventories at power stations were equivalent to only 5.9 days of consumption, against 14.7 days a year earlier. Supramaxes have been hardest hit, with Indian-bound coal volumes falling 16%, compared with a 4% decline for panamaxes. October offered the first signs of a turn, with Indian seaborne coal arrivals rising 7% year-on-year. However, BIMCO expects only a limited import recovery in 2027 as domestic mining grows.

items.title: Hapag’s standalone Asia-Mexico string adds another spoke to Gemini hub network
items.original_title: Hapag’s standalone Asia-Mexico string adds another spoke to Gemini hub network
items.summary: Hapag-Lloyd has presented AMX, its new Asia–Mexico service, as standalone: its own ships; its own rotation of Ningbo-Qingdao-Busan-Ensenada-Manzanillo-Lázaro Cárdenas-Ningbo; launching in January 2027. Standalone is the word the press release leans on, and it is the one worth questioning. AMX is standalone the way a spoke is standalone – Hapag owns the vessels, but it can only fill an 8,000 teu ship on this run because the Gemini hub network it operates with Maersk gives the cargo somewhere to come from. The hub-and-spoke network it now runs with Maersk supplies the missing pieces – balancing cargo through the Gemini hubs and relay connections onward, so AMX does not have to source a full, self-sufficient ship at Asian load ports. The simple answer to ‘why standalone’ and ‘why 2027’ is that the network to support a self-controlled spoke only recently came together. Each is an owned loop made to clip onto the Gemini backbone, and the method is consistent — control the vessel, fill it through the hubs. That slice is not small: I estimate Hapag’s allocation on MSC’s loops is worth around 8,375 teu of nominal vessel capacity, call it some 7,000 teu of usable space for its customers once a ship is realistically loaded.

items.title: Panama Canal turns the taps back on
items.original_title: Panama Canal turns the taps back on
items.summary: The Panama Canal has raised its daily transit capacity to 34 vessels and increased the maximum allowable draft for neopanamax ships to 50 ft, marking another significant easing of restrictions following an exceptionally wet October. The Panama Canal Authority (ACP) confirmed that an additional booking slot for super-category vessels at the original panamax locks would increase their daily allocation from 18 to 19. Total availability now stands at 24 slots through the panamax locks and 10 through the larger neopanamax locks, up from a combined 33 previously. The maximum neopanamax draft has meanwhile increased from 49 ft to 50 ft (15.24 m), effective immediately and until further notice. Data compiled by Ursa Shipbrokers showed Gatun Lake averaged 85.80 ft (26.15 m) during October, just 0.15 ft below its historical average and more than 6 ft higher than during the drought-stricken October of 2023. Rainfall across the canal watershed during the first 29 days of October was 8.4% above the 30-year average and 83.6% greater than the corresponding period three years ago. The turnaround is particularly striking given the dire outlook during August, when weak rainfall and a strengthening El Niño forced authorities to slash daily booking capacity to 32 vessels and impose tighter draft restrictions.

items.title: Korea shipbuilders face LNG carrier price squeeze as North America orders seen next year
items.original_title: Korea shipbuilders face LNG carrier price squeeze as North America orders seen next year
items.summary: LNG carriers are the flagship high-margin vessel type where Korean shipbuilders have shown strength. According to Clarksons Research, the ship new building price for a 174,000-cubic-meter LNG carrier fell from an average of $248 million in January this year to $245 million in October. In fact, contract prices for newbuild LNG carriers at Samsung Heavy Industries, which has the most LNG carrier orders among Korean shipbuilders, have dropped from late last year and early this year. At its third-quarter earnings briefing on the 29th of last month, Samsung Heavy Industries acknowledged it had recently taken LNG carrier orders at low prices. Some analysts say China’s rising share of LNG carrier orders is pressuring Korean shipbuilders to lower prices. On the decline in Korea’s market share and prices due to China’s rising LNG carrier orders, Samsung Heavy Industries said it is “carefully monitoring developments in China.” Bae Gi-yeon, an analyst at Meritz Securities, said, “Capacity expansion and new entrants at Chinese shipyards are putting downward pressure on the ship new building price for LNG carriers,” adding, “The pricing competitiveness of low-cost LNG carriers from Chinese shipyards is bound to stand out.” The broader base of Chinese yards is forcing Korean shipbuilders to cut prices to win orders.

items.original_title: Carriers may secure only part of their November rate increases as Suez returns, Sogese report says
items.summary: Freight rates to Europe have rebounded since early October after falling steadily from their July peak, but the conditions behind the rebound are mixed. Cargo demand is positive, with Far East to Europe volumes up 12.2% in the first seven months of the year, according to Xeneta. Ships, however, are arriving late, and the return of Suez routings is releasing capacity faster than schedules are recovering. In its November Europe Container Market Update, Sogese reads this as a market moving from a disruption premium to a capacity-management test, in which the price carriers announce and the price shippers actually pay are drifting apart. If Suez keeps normalising, the key question for 2027 will not be whether there are enough ships, but how aggressively carriers manage the capacity that comes back into the market.”Andrea Monti, CEO & MD, Sogese 2. For its November outlook the report also sets out three paths: partial uptake of announced increases, failure of the increases to reach market rates, and uneven capacity and pricing as Suez rotations are rebuilt. items.title: Ports of LA/LB, watchmen extend contract through 20 November as negotiations continue
items.original_title: Ports of LA/LB, watchmen extend contract through 20 November as negotiations continue
items.summary: Negotiations continue amid an effort to avoid a work stoppage at the West Coast ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach (LA/LB), and the union and the ports have agreed to extend their contract through 20 November. International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) Local 26, the union representing about 250 port watchmen at the ports of LA/LB, and the Pacific Maritime Association (PMA), which represents employers, will continue negotiating a new contract during the extension. Should the watchmen strike, operations at eight terminals in the port complex could be brought to a halt. Watchmen make up only 2% of ILWU workers at the two ports but work at terminals handling roughly 85% of Long Beach’s cargo and 33% of Los Angeles’ cargo. It is the third extension after the watchmen originally planned to strike on 4 November. Negotiations will continue with the assistance of the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service (FMCS), PMA said in a statement on its website. The watchmen are not part of the agreement reached in 2023 between 29 West Coast ports and 22,000 workers that expires in 2028. Titanium dioxide (TiO2) is also shipped in containers. China, the world’s biggest oil buyer, imported 41.94 million metric tons of crude oil in October, or 9.88 million barrels per day, ⁠with the daily ⁠import rate up 9.4% from September, according to data from the General Administration of Customs. China’s oil product exports, including gasoline, diesel, jet fuel and fuel oil, fell to 5.18 million ⁠tons in October from 7.16 million tons in September, but were up 14.6% from a year earlier, according to the data. Refined oil product exports in the first 10 months of the year totaled 46.59 million tons, down 2% from a year earlier. Oil product imports rose to 3.15 million tons in October from ⁠1.85 ⁠million tons in September. January-to-October imports fell to 27.15 million tons from 34.19 million tons a year earlier. Data also showed that natural gas imports, including liquefied natural gas and pipeline gas, rose 2.4% from a year earlier to 10.01 million tons in October. items.original_title: U.S. Formalizes Two-Month Extension of China Ship Port Fee Suspension
items.summary: The Trump administration has formally extended its suspension of port fees targeting Chinese-built and Chinese-operated vessels for another two months, keeping the controversial measures on hold while Washington continues trade negotiations with Beijing. The decision, published Tuesday in the Federal Register, extends the suspension through 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on January 9, 2027, with the measures potentially resuming January 10 unless further action is taken. The extension took effect November 9, preventing the fees from returning following the expiration of an earlier one-year suspension agreed to under a trade deal between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in November 2025. The extension also maintains the suspension of additional duties on Chinese ship-to-shore cranes and other cargo-handling equipment. USTR said it will continue monitoring China’s maritime and shipbuilding practices and consider whether to extend the suspension again or take further action before the January 10 deadline. The decision comes as China has also extended its suspension of retaliatory port fees targeting U.S.-linked vessels until January 10, 2027, according to a Reuters report on Monday. China also extended its suspension of an investigation into the security of shipping and shipbuilding supply chains.

items.title: ‘Nonsense Rate’: Iran War Exposes Turmoil Behind Key Tanker Benchmark

items.summary: By Jack Farchy and Alex Longley (Bloomberg) — In March this year, inside a 282-year-old institution responsible for one of the most important prices in global oil markets, one man staged a quiet protest. “Nonsense rate,” Christopher Loveday wrote on March 23 in an internal document at the Baltic Exchange, where he was responsible for helping produce the world’s benchmark rate for shipping oil. “Still a nonsense,” he wrote two days later. Collectively, they offer unprecedented insight into how the war in Iran played out inside a key corner of the global oil market. It has shown that numerous people involved in the key oil tanker rate, called TD3C, expressed reservations as the Baltic Exchange continued to publish the price in the early weeks of the war. Still, there were hopes that the war may end quickly, and when the Baltic held a call for its panelist brokers on March 4, the conclusion was that they were willing to keep submitting assessments. Still, he also said in court that he had thought since the start of the war that TD3C should have been suspended.

items.summary: Hapag-Lloyd, the world’s fifth-largest container carrier, operates 300 vessels on 133 liner services, transporting 13.5 million twenty-foot-equivalent units a year between 600 ports worldwide. Given the scale and complexity of these operations, every decision affects thousands of containers per vessel – with the consequences of any misstep felt throughout the supply chain. The company’s proactive approach to fleetwide digitalisation has therefore been devised with one overarching objective in mind: to simplify its operations. “We digitalise because there’s a use case for it – because there’s value we can drive.” For Hapag-Lloyd, tangible targets include maintaining schedule reliability above 90% across its network, reducing emissions per TEU by 30% by 2030, and approaching net-zero emissions by 2045 – all while cutting operating costs by approximately $100 per TEU. In this way, Briest explained, Hapag-Lloyd could keep commercial and environmental impacts to a minimum without compromising voyage safety. Digitalisation and connectivity, then, enable shipping companies like Hapag-Lloyd to make smarter operational decisions based on a richer and more immediate view of what is happening on the vessel and across the network. In a further operational scenario from the notional voyage, Briest explained that the Hapag-Lloyd LIVE tool allows customers to monitor refrigerated cargo and respond when circumstances change.

The analyst expects average annual fleet growth of 10% between 2027 and 2030, based on existing orders, with further newbuilding contracts potentially increasing that figure. Quarterly deliveries are forecast to average 1m teu over the period, peaking at 1.8m teu in the third quarter of 2028. This compares with average quarterly deliveries of 560,000 teu between 2023 and 2026, highlighting the scale of capacity due to enter the market. In 2016, carriers scrapped a record 670,000 teu, equivalent to just 3.3% of the fleet, during the industry’s previous overcapacity crisis. Jonathan Roach, analyst at Braemar, told The Loadstar there were 1,944 vessels aged 20 years or more, with 1,903 ships on order. Jan Tiedemann, VP liner strategy at Alphaliner, told The Loadstar he expected scrapping to increase in 2027 and 2028 without offsetting the newbuilding influx. He also pointed to the replacement needs of larger vessels built between 2000 and 2010, many of which will approach the end of their commercial lives in the mid-2030s.

items.title: UK offshore supply chain looks overseas for growth
items.original_title: UK offshore supply chain looks overseas for growth
items.summary: The UK’s offshore energy supply chain is increasingly looking overseas for new business as uncertainty surrounding domestic projects threatens investment, jobs and specialist engineering capacity, according to a new industry report. Offshore Energies UK (OEUK) found that just 35% of 60 companies surveyed were confident about their UK business prospects over the next 12 months. Meanwhile, 80% expect more future investment and growth to come from international markets. The findings form part of OEUK’s Supply Chain Report 2026, which examines the pressures facing engineering companies, manufacturers, vessel operators, logistics providers, and other businesses supporting offshore energy developments. The trade body identified approximately £123bn ($165.5bn) of potential UK offshore energy capital investment between 2026 and 2035 but warned that many projects remain uncertain. According to the report, 95% of companies surveyed believe they could expand capacity if domestic offshore activity increased. OEUK warned that offshore wind, carbon capture, and other emerging energy markets have not yet generated sufficient activity to replace traditional oil and gas work at scale. Katy Heidenreich, OEUK’s supply chain and people director, called for continued investment in domestic oil and gas alongside renewable energy developments. OEUK cautioned that losing specialist offshore capabilities now could leave the UK increasingly dependent on overseas suppliers when future energy projects move into construction.

items.summary: MSC-controlled Global Car Carriers (GCC) has expanded its newbuilding programme to 26 LNG dual-fuel car carriers, adding four more 8,600 ceu vessels at Chinese yards as the Oslo-based owner presses ahead with one of the sector’s largest fleet renewal drives. The former Gram Car Carriers has listed two additional ships at Zhoushan Changhong International Shipyard, with both scheduled for completion in 2030. A further pair has been assigned to China Merchants’ Weihai yard, with completion dates in 2031. All four vessels have capacity for 8,600 vehicles and LNG dual-fuel propulsion, according to GCC’s updated fleet records. The additions take GCC’s newbuilding programme to 22 vessels of 8,600 ceu and four of 7,000 ceu, representing combined nominal capacity of 217,200 ceu. Splash reported in October that GCC had added two 8,600 ceu car carriers at Changhong, bringing its orderbook at the time to 22 ships. The latest four vessels increase that programme by another 34,400 vehicle spaces and push the delivery schedule into 2031. GCC’s expansion has gathered pace since Mediterranean Shipping Company acquired Oslo-listed Gram Car Carriers in 2024 in a transaction worth around $700m. The Aponte-controlled group subsequently took the company private, with Gram adopting the Global Car Carriers name earlier this year.

We also explore the growing impact of port congestion, as typhoons and operational disruption put further pressure on already stretched supply chains, plus the contrasting developments in the Middle East with increasing returns to Red Sea transits and continued uncertainty around the Strait of Hormuz. Finally, we revisit the predictions made in our Q2 episode to see how they measured up, before asking Nigel and Gavin to look ahead and share their forecasts for the coming months. items.original_title: South Korea clears Sinar Mas takeover of Hyundai LNG Shipping
items.summary: South Korea has given conditional approval for the sale of Hyundai LNG Shipping to Indonesia’s Sinar Mas Group, removing the final regulatory hurdle in a deal that has been held up for months by national energy security concerns. The Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy has completed a foreign investment security review, approving the transaction subject to undisclosed national security conditions. The sellers, a consortium comprising IMM Private Equity and IMM Investment, are now targeting November 23 to complete the transaction, nearly a year after signing a sale agreement with Sinar Mas. Hyundai LNG Shipping operates 12 LNG carriers and six LPG carriers and holds long-term transportation contracts with state-owned Korea Gas Corporation (KOGAS). The proposed foreign takeover has faced fierce opposition from South Korean shipowners, who warned that transferring control of strategically important gas carriers overseas could undermine national energy security and lead to the loss of maritime expertise. Sinar Mas has sought to address these concerns by pledging to maintain Korean-flag operations and protect existing employment. Hyundai LNG Shipping was carved out of Hyundai Merchant Marine, now HMM, in 2014. An attempt to sell the business back to HMM in 2023 collapsed over differences in valuation. The latest approval clears the way for IMM to exit its investment after 12 years.

items.summary: The Baltic Exchange’s dry bulk freight index, which tracks rates for ships carrying dry bulk commodities, was up for a fourth session on Monday, rising by 1.8% to its highest since October 9 at 2,854 points. items.summary: A shipbroker contributed US$24,000 towards a settlement of a demurrage dispute after delays in forwarding key documents complicated a claim between shipowners and charterers, according to a case highlighted by International Transport Intermediaries Club (ITIC) in its most recent Claims Review. The dispute concerned a demurrage claim, valued at approximately US$48,000, which the owners were pursuing against charterers for delays at discharge. The shipbroker became involved after failing to pass on supporting documents relating to the claim. However, the broker’s delay in forwarding key documents meant the charterers’ objections did not reach the owners promptly, reducing the opportunity to address any deficiencies in the claim. Given the weaknesses in the underlying demurrage claim, the matter was settled with the shipbroker contributing US$24,000, half the value of the claim, towards the owners’ losses. “In this case, the delay reduced the owners’ chance to deal with problems in their claim early. Expert support in assessing liability and negotiating a resolution can make a real difference to the result. Demurrage claims often carry tight contractual time bars, so claims and supporting documents should be passed on as soon as they arrive, with a record of when that happened. Even a short delay can prejudice a party’s position and prove costly.” Source: International Transport Intermediaries Club (ITIC)

The initiative aims to improve intelligence sharing, strengthen cooperation between port and customs authorities, and better identify shipping routes and containers being exploited by criminal organizations. items.title: Cargo boycott threat by Indian brokers over empty-box fee hikes
items.original_title: Cargo boycott threat by Indian brokers over empty-box fee hikes
items.summary: A new storm of stakeholder disputes, and potential operational disruption, is brewing across Indian ports over policy changes by container lines on empty-container handling and associated depot charges. The loading and unloading of empty boxes at yards is the flashpoint for discontent and disagreement between supply chain intermediaries and carriers. Maersk, for example, has substantially raised its lift-on/lift-off (lo-lo) charges for empties moving via Mundra, India’s busiest container port and the primary gateway for the hinterlands around Delhi. The revision, implemented from 1 November, effectively more than doubled the rates shippers had been charged, from $23 to $51 per 20ft empty box, and from $31 to $67 per 40ft, plus local taxes. Ondeed, one liner source told The Loadstar : “We are discussing the matter.” At Chennai, MSC seems to be facing the brunt of a trade pushback against the practice of routing empty tariff collections through third-party depot vendors, which cargo agents claim opens the market to an unregulated environment. “MSC has taken the lead in implementing this collection practice in Chennai, following which other shipping lines have initiated similar measures,” the Chennai Customs Brokers Association (CCBA) noted. The CCBA claimed the policy shift was fraught with “serious economic and operational implications for cargo agents”, as it had seen third-party vendors keep inflating tariffs once taken over.

items.title: IMO faces calls to enhance maritime security code amid rising threats
items.original_title: IMO faces calls to enhance maritime security code amid rising threats
items.summary: The International Association of Ports and Harbors has called on the International Maritime Organization to update the world’s main maritime security regulatory framework, as escalating attacks on commercial shipping and emerging cyber and technology risks expose potential gaps in rules largely unchanged for more than two decades. In a statement Nov. 5, the industry group representing roughly 400 ports and related businesses globally said there was a case for updated guidance around the International Ship and Port Facility Security Code to reflect modern port operations and strengthen cooperation between governments and industry. The debate comes amid severe disruption to key energy shipping routes amid persistent security concerns. Jeremy Greenwood, head of the IMO’s Maritime Security Section, welcomed further discussion on the ISPS code but stressed that increasing threats did not necessarily mean the regulation itself was fundamentally flawed. Adopted in 2002 and mandatory since 2004 under the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea, the ISPS Code sets security requirements for ships and ports, covering access controls, threat assessments, security plans and operational procedures. Code revamp A US proposal this year said the code had not undergone a significant revision since adoption despite evolving security threats to merchant shipping. The IMO is due to hold the next meeting of the Maritime Safety Committee during Dec.

items.title: India’s coking coal import dependence on Australia falls to 54%
items.original_title: India’s coking coal import dependence on Australia falls to 54%
items.summary: India’s dependence on Australia for coking coal imports fell to 54% in 2025 from 73% in 2019, according to a deposition by the steel ministry to a parliamentary standing committee. About 90% of India’s coking coal requirement, a key raw material for steelmaking via the BF-BOF route, is met through imports because India has limited availability of high-quality, low-ash coking coal. Australia remains India’s largest source of coking coal imports, but the share of Russia rose from 0.62% to 8.15%, the US from 8% to 17%, Mozambique from 4% to 7.31% and Indonesia from 2.46% to 4%. India’s steel sector imported 58 Mt of coking coal in FY25, up from 57 Mt in FY24, at a cost of around Rs 1.5 lakh crore. Under the Aatmanirbhar Coal Mission, the government’s Mission Coking Coal targets 140 Mt of domestic raw coking coal production by 2030 – 105 Mt from Coal India Limited and 35 Mt from private allocations – while aiming to raise the blending ratio of domestic coal in steelmaking from 10% to 30%. Globally, high-quality hard coking coal is concentrated in a few countries, and Australia accounts for more than 50% of internationally traded coking coal owing to its high-quality reserves, stable mining ecosystem and efficient logistics. Source: SMM

items.summary: Spanish towage giant Boluda has acquired Dutch offshore towage and heavy transport specialist Muller Dordrecht, adding 16 tugs and eight barges to its growing global fleet. The takeover gives Boluda full ownership of the century-old family business, whose fleet includes seven offshore tugs specialising in complex marine transportation, rig moves, anchor handling and offshore wind projects. Financial terms of the transaction have not been disclosed. Muller, founded in 1918 and headquartered in Dordrecht, will continue operating as an independent unit under the name Boluda Muller Towage, retaining its existing management team and focusing on offshore towage and marine projects worldwide. The Dutch operator has built a sizeable presence in the North Sea and Baltic markets, supporting offshore energy and infrastructure projects ranging from transporting wind turbine foundations and offshore substations to heavy lifting and coastal towage. Its fleet includes the 120-tonne bollard pull En Avant 30 and the 90-tonne bollard pull En Avant 25 and En Avant 26 , which can operate both offshore and in ports. Boluda Towage executive chairman Vicente Boluda Ceballos said the acquisition would broaden the group’s specialist offshore capabilities while allowing Muller to continue developing its operations alongside Boluda’s existing European business.

The ownership change gives Moscow greater control over a critical part of the supply chain for its Arctic energy projects, from transporting construction modules to remote project sites to potentially delivering finished LNG infrastructure to future overseas customers. The development comes as two other Chinese heavy-lift carriers with connections to Russian Arctic shipping have attracted attention off Norway’s northern coast near Andøya . items.title: Record supply growth pushes container fleet towards 50m teu by 2030
items.original_title: Record supply growth pushes container fleet towards 50m teu by 2030
items.summary: The global containership fleet is heading towards an unprecedented 50m teu by 2030, setting the stage for a potentially devastating oversupply crisis and enormous downward pressure on freight rates. New analysis from Sea-Intelligence shows the fleet expanding from today’s 34m teu to 40m teu by the second quarter of 2028 and 50m teu by the third quarter of 2030, the largest capacity expansion in container shipping history. Combined with an estimated 8% effective capacity boost from the return of Asia-Europe services to the Suez Canal, cumulative supply growth could exceed 50% by the end of the decade. The consultancy calculates that quarterly newbuilding deliveries will average 1m teu between 2027 and 2030, peaking at an extraordinary 1.8m teu in the third quarter of 2028. Even if carriers repeated the record demolition levels of 2016 every year through 2030, this would absorb less than 17% of incoming capacity, leaving annual fleet growth averaging 8.5%. By 2030, some 10.8m teu will be aboard ships older than 20 years, although Sea-Intelligence doubts carriers intend to scrap anything approaching that figure. The warnings follow a similarly bearish forecast from Xeneta, which expects fleet growth of 6.8% next year against demand growth of just 2.5% to 4%.

items.title: Black Sea shipping reels from fresh attacks and record insurance costs
items.original_title: Black Sea shipping reels from fresh attacks and record insurance costs
items.summary: The Black Sea has experienced another violent weekend, with Russia claiming fresh strikes on merchant ships, human remains discovered aboard a damaged tanker in Bulgaria and war-risk insurance premiums reaching an extraordinary 20% of hull value. Russia’s defence ministry issued a succession of statements over the weekend claiming to have attacked commercial vessels carrying military supplies for Ukraine. On Saturday, Moscow reported hitting a dry cargo ship southeast of Odesa, followed by another claim involving a vessel east of the Ukrainian port. Romanian radar detected two aerial targets near Snake Island on Sunday, prompting Spanish F-18 fighters and NH90 helicopters to scramble from the Mihail Kogălniceanu airbase. Bulgaria, Romania and Turkey activated their joint Black Sea mine-countermeasures group on Saturday, with vessels participating in the Poseidon 2026 exercise off Bulgaria. The mounting attacks are producing unprecedented insurance costs. Black Sea war-risk insurance premiums have reached as much as 20% of vessel value for particularly exposed voyages, according to insurance market sources, exceeding even the extraordinary rates seen during the Iran-Iraq tanker war of the 1980s. For comparison, historical research from the University of Texas and contemporary reporting from the London insurance market show tanker-war premiums reaching 7.5% and occasionally exceeding 10% during the 1980s.

items.summary: Greek shipowner Panos Efthimiadis is making his first move into dry bulk shipping, with his Leon Shipping & Trading linked to a kamsarmax newbuilding at China’s Hengli Heavy Industries as its orderbook grows to five vessels. The Athens-based company has also been linked to two LR1 product tanker newbuildings, adding to a pair of 50,000 dwt MR tankers recently booked at Cosco Shipping Heavy Industry (Guangdong). Details of the LR1 contracts, including the shipyard, delivery dates and pricing, have yet to emerge. Pricing has not been disclosed, although current market assessments put similar MR newbuildings at around $53m each, suggesting a combined benchmark of approximately $106m. Brokers have linked the 2008-built, 50,000 dwt Leon Wisdom to a $26m sale to Union Maritime, while sistership Leon Grace was sold last month for a reported $23.5m to UAE interests and subsequently renamed Bella Sky . Both vessels were acquired earlier this year from International Seaways for a combined $32m. The reported sales would therefore generate approximately $17.5m above their original purchase prices, before transaction and other costs. Efthimiadis established Leon Shipping & Trading in 2010 after spending 22 years with family-owned Lotus Shipping. The Hengli contract would mark its first investment in dry bulk tonnage, adding a new segment to its fleet renewal and expansion programme.

items.summary: Lila Global, GMS’s shipowning arm, is expanding its presence in the ageing LNG carrier market, adding its third LNG carrier since September. While the first two acquisitions were steam-powered vessels, the latest addition features a dual-fuel diesel-electric (DFDE) propulsion system. The first vessel to join the fleet was the 2003-built, steam-powered Castillo de Villalba, renamed Carla. Earlier this month, Splash reported that the 18-year-old, steam-powered LNG carrier Tangguh Batur (145,700 cu m) had been sold to Lila Global for $30m and renamed Eagle M. Now, Splash can report that Lila Global has added a third LNG carrier to its fleet: the 17-year-old, DFDE-powered Diamond, formerly Kmarin Diamond. Brokers report that the vessel changed hands for $65m, more than double the price paid for Eagle M.

items.title: Russia Says It Hit Three Cargo Ships In Black Sea
items.original_title: Russia Says It Hit Three Cargo Ships In Black Sea
items.summary: A cargo vessel leaves a port in the Black Sea, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Odesa, Ukraine March 26, 2025. REUTERS/Nina Liashonok MOSCOW, Nov 8 (Reuters) – Russia said on Sunday overnight strikes by its forces had hit three cargo vessels that were carrying military goods for Ukraine and two electricity substations, which it said supplied power to the Ukrainian defense industry. The Defence Ministry said Russian forces had struck a container ship delivering weapons and military equipment to the Black Sea port of Odesa, and another in the port of Chornomorsk, which is in the same southwestern region of Ukraine. It said a third vessel, a dry cargo ship hit south-west of Odesa, was carrying weapons and military equipment for Ukraine’s armed forces. The ministry also said Russia had hit two power substations in Ukraine’s Dnipropetrovsk and Zhytomyr regions, both of which it said powered military-industrial enterprises. Ukrainian power company DTEK said a Russian overnight attack on energy facilities in Dnipropetrovsk had left more than 600,000 people without electricity. After seven strikes on cargo ships near NATO members Romania and Bulgaria last month, the US-led military alliance said it would deploy maritime patrol aircraft, radars and drones to bolster its eastern flank in the Black Sea.

The 2002-built VLCC Era, better known until recently as Marinera and before that Bella 1, had resurfaced under the Comoros flag after another change of identity. Sources say it was sold at a huge discount by the US for $205 per ldt. For comparison, GMS’s latest report notes that tankers are fetching $535 per ldt in Bangladesh and that buying appetite remains healthy, particularly in Bangladesh, although the persistent shortage of available candidates continues to prevent stronger sentiment from translating into fresh transactions. items.title: Banks step up pressure on Havila Shipping over $78m debt dispute
items.original_title: Banks step up pressure on Havila Shipping over $78m debt dispute
items.summary: Norwegian offshore vessel owner Havila Shipping is facing renewed enforcement action from three major banks seeking to establish security liens over the company’s assets in connection with a long-running debt restructuring dispute. DNB, Swedbank, and Danske Bank have submitted a new request for attachment liens covering NOK779m ($78m), comprising NOK713m in principal and approximately NOK65m in accrued interest. The latest move follows a ruling by Norway’s Borgarting Court of Appeal on October 19, which went against Havila in its dispute with the lenders over a restructuring agreement dating back to 2020. Havila has said it disagrees with the judgment and intends to appeal to the Norwegian Supreme Court. The deadline for filing the appeal is November 19. The dispute centres on whether Havila breached the restructuring agreement by refinancing debt owed to lenders that had opted for a cash settlement in December 2024. The three banks, which financed the offshore support vessels Havila Foresight and Havila Harmony , maintain that the refinancing violated the agreement and have since demanded repayment of the outstanding debt. Havila has disputed the lenders’ interpretation, arguing that the banks were obliged to convert certain non-interest-bearing debt tranches into shares under the restructuring arrangements.

items.title: Meyer Werft sets up offshore business to handle $2.8bn converter orderbook
items.original_title: Meyer Werft sets up offshore business to handle $2.8bn converter orderbook
items.summary: German shipbuilding group Meyer Werft is setting up a dedicated offshore business to manage its growing involvement in North Sea converter platform construction. The new company, Neptun Offshore, will bring together the group’s offshore converter activities and hold its 50% stake in Neptun Smulders Offshore Renewables (NSORe), a joint venture with Belgian steel construction specialist Smulders. NSORe secured two major offshore converter contracts from German transmission system operator 50Hertz earlier this year for the LanWin3 and LanWin6 grid connection projects in the North Sea. The joint venture’s share of the contracts is valued at approximately €2.5bn ($2.8bn), with a substantial proportion of the work expected to take place in the German state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, including at Neptun Werft’s facilities in Rostock. Both projects involve 2GW offshore converter platforms designed to transmit electricity generated by North Sea wind farms to the German power grid. Meyer Werft said the decision to establish a separate company reflects the different technical, regulatory and financial requirements of converter platform construction compared with conventional shipbuilding. Neptun Offshore will be a wholly owned subsidiary of Meyer Werft, headed by Malte Poelmann, who already serves as managing director of NSORe alongside Dieter Weyns. The group aims to have the new structure established ahead of the construction of the first converter platform in 2028.

items.original_title: IMO Council urges stronger protection of seafarers amid threats to global shipping
items.summary: Council condemns attacks on merchant shipping in the Red Sea and Black Sea, mourns loss of 25th seafarer since onset of Strait of Hormuz conflict, and renews Secretary-General’s tenure. items.title: Egypt’s October wheat imports nearly triple, corn imports fall 35%
items.original_title: Egypt’s October wheat imports nearly triple, corn imports fall 35%
items.summary: Egypt imported 985,425 metric tons of wheat in October 2026, according to local shipping data from LATT Trading & Shipping, nearly tripling September’s total but down 47% year over year. Russia regained its position as Egypt’s largest supplier in October, shipping 403,245 mt, up 272% month on month. Russian wheat exported from the Baltic became more prominent: Latvian ports supplied 107,819 mt and a Lithuanian port supplied 30,700 mt, accounting for 14% of October imports. Ukrainian wheat arrivals almost doubled to 269,070 mt from September, representing 27% of October imports. The fall in prices was also driven by the state’s sales of wheat to private mills at EGP 16,650/mt, lower than the ex-warehouse prices. Corn imports fall on currency fluctuations, sufficient stocks Egypt’s corn imports totaled 777,269 metric tons in October 2026, down 35% month over month and 42.2% year over year, according to local shipping data from LATT Trading & Shipping. Market participants consequently expect imports to slow further in November, with one importer estimating Brazilian arrivals at around 450,000 mt. Platts-assessed Ukrainian corn averaged $220.81/mt in October, down $3.59/mt from $224.40/mt in September. Platts-assessed Brazilian corn averaged $223.82/mt in October, down $16.67/mt from $240.49/mt in September, and Argentine corn averaged $216.70/mt in October, down $9.39/mt from $226.10/mt in September.

items.title: HPCL Struggles To Book Tankers For Hormuz Crude
items.original_title: HPCL Struggles To Book Tankers For Hormuz Crude
items.summary: Vessel shortages and last-minute withdrawals by shipowners complicate crude shipments from the Persian Gulf despite recovering regional supplies Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd (HPCL) is facing difficulties securing tankers to transport crude from inside the Persian Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz, as vessel shortages and last-minute withdrawals by shipowners complicate shipment arrangements, according to media reports. The challenge persists even as crude supplies from the Middle East recover and more vessels resume crossings through the strategic waterway. HPCL Chairman Vikas Kaushal said in an interview in Abu Dhabi this week that finding ships for available loading dates remains difficult, with some shipowners withdrawing even after agreeing to transport cargoes. HPCL bought an average of about 2,40,000 barrels per day of Middle Eastern crude in 2025, according to data from energy intelligence provider Kpler. The volume declined to 57,000 barrels per day in April 2026, when the conflict severely disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Purchases subsequently recovered to an average of 256,000 barrels per day in October as more supplies from the region became available, Kpler data showed. The arrangement allows buyers to access regional supplies without having to independently arrange vessels for the entire journey from within the Gulf. For HPCL, the ability to procure crude and secure transportation for it remain distinct challenges.

items.title: China copper premium hits record as market weighs US stock shift

items.summary: Concerns over the potential redistribution of large copper stocks accumulated in the US are rising among China-based market participants, with any return of metal to the international market potentially reshaping global trade flows as China’s copper import premium hits a record high amid tightening domestic availability. The market is facing competing pressures, with expectations that easing US tariff risks could release more metal into the international market and pressure futures prices, while physical tightness in China continues to support spot premiums and demand for imported cathode. China’s copper cathode import premium rose to an all-time high Nov. Platts, part of S&P Global Energy, assessed the Chinese copper import premium at $220/metric ton over the London Metal Exchange cash price, CIF China, on Nov. The record premium comes as market participants reassess international copper flows following the US midterm elections, with China-based market participants increasingly expecting a potential delay or moderation in US tariffs on refined copper imports in 2027. The spread between COMEX and LME copper prices narrowed to about minus $85/mt as of Nov. “The price spread is key, while logistics and domestic US demand will create friction.” Copper prices came under pressure recently as the market reassessed US tariff expectations following the midterm election results, according to China-based market sources.

items.title: Stowaway prevention: best practice
items.original_title: Stowaway prevention: best practice
items.summary: Stowaways remain a significant security and operational risk for vessels calling at ports in West Africa. Two recent cases handled by Skuld once again highlight the persistent stowaway risk in the region and the importance of conducting thorough and systematic physical searches. Even where professional third-party security services and trained search dogs are employed, the vessel’s own search remains a critical element of effective stowaway prevention. Best practices For vessels calling at ports with an elevated stowaway risk, Skuld recommends a layered approach centred on access control and systematic physical searches. Importantly, sufficient time must be allocated for each stowaway search. Ultimately, effective stowaway prevention depends not on completing a checklist or obtaining a search certificate, but on ensuring that the vessel has been thoroughly searched. Loss prevention recommendations The company should establish clear stowaway search procedures appropriate to each vessel’s trade, type and operating conditions. Effective implementation of the above best practices and recommendations can significantly reduce the risk of stowaways gaining access to or remaining undetected on board. A well-planned and properly executed stowaway prevention programme not only reduces the likelihood of operational disruption, delay and associated costs, but also contributes to the safety and security of the vessel and her crew throughout the voyage.

items.title: South Korea tests Arctic shipping route amid Russia-West row
items.original_title: South Korea tests Arctic shipping route amid Russia-West row
items.summary: A South Korean container ship completed a voyage to Western Europe through the Arctic Ocean off the northern coast of Russia in October, fueling Seoul’s hopes of exploiting the route as a shortcut for trade. The ship made the round trip from Busan to Rotterdam in just 50 days, saving at least 10 days compared to the fastest travel times along the more commonly used Suez Canal route. The Northern Sea Route (NSR) is not only around 7,000 kilometers (4,350 miles) shorter, it also avoids the geopolitical flashpoint of the Middle East. One of the reasons for South Korea testing the Arctic route is its undoubtedly large economic potential. “In addition to potentially lowering shipping costs and transit times, the route’s development could strengthen Busan’s position as a regional maritime hub and create opportunities for South Korea’s shipbuilding sector.” The Lee government has outlined plans for regular commercial services on the NSR by 2030, with the first Korean ship to complete the voyage merely a test of the logistics. Fears of ‘strategic dependency’ The danger, however, is that by developing the NSR as South Korea’s favored route to Europe, “it could introduce a new form of strategic dependency on Russia as Moscow exercises considerable control over navigation along its Arctic coastline,” said Kristanto.

items.title: Turkey’s coal dependence faces scrutiny as COP31 climate summit begins
items.original_title: Turkey’s coal dependence faces scrutiny as COP31 climate summit begins
items.summary: Turkey’s reliance on coal is facing renewed scrutiny ahead of the COP31 climate summit, as communities affected by mining operations urge world leaders to examine the environmental damage linked to the country’s largest electricity source. The United Nations climate conference begins Monday in Antalya and runs through November 20, with the transition toward cleaner energy among the central issues under discussion. Residents of Ikizkoy, near the Akbelen forest in southwestern Mugla province, want delegates to visit communities affected by decades of lignite mining and the expansion of nearby coal operations. Coal generated 34% of Turkey’s electricity last year, making the country Europe’s largest producer of coal-fired power, according to energy research group Ember. Mining operations around Akbelen supply the Yenikoy and Kemerkoy power plants, which together generate slightly more than 2% of Turkey’s electricity. Turkey is proposing a voluntary global electrification target at COP31, although its climate benefits would depend on whether additional electricity comes from low-carbon sources. Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar acknowledged the difficulties of reducing coal dependence, citing thousands of jobs supported by mining operations. Ankara considers nuclear power a major alternative and aims to develop 10 gigawatts of nuclear generation capacity by 2040, roughly equivalent to the country’s current coal-powered output.

The Loadstar managing editor Gavin van Marle joins us fresh from the World Ports Conference in London to discuss the key talking points from the event, the latest concerns around potential disruption at the Los Angeles and Long Beach ports, and what the return of container services to the Suez Canal could mean for shipping rates and congestion. We also examine why the transpacific trade remains so lucrative for carriers. Then, new TIACA director general Mammen Tharakan joins us to discuss the air cargo market, including tight capacity and strong demand on the transpacific, the potential impact of returning Middle Eastern capacity, and how ongoing instability around the Strait of Hormuz is affecting market confidence and contracting decisions. From port disruption and Suez transits to the air cargo capacity crunch, we bring you up to speed on the stories driving the freight industry this week. This article is © The Loadstar. items.summary: CAIRO, Nov 8 (Reuters) – Egyptian fertilizer producers have been notified of a new 33% reduction in their natural gas supplies, a company statement and industry officials said on Sunday, as the country seeks to curb the need for expensive liquefied natural gas imports. Misr Fertilizers Production Company MFPC.CA said it had been told of the reduction, which follows an earlier 20% cut to gas supplies for fertilizer plants. Egypt relies on domestic gas and, increasingly, imported LNG for power generation, but domestic output has struggled to keep pace with rising demand. The ministry budgeted about $10.1 billion for LNG in the 2026/27 financial year, but prices have run above its estimates, an analyst said in October. It had spent $5.8 billion by October 6, putting it on course to overrun the budget before demand usually rises in spring and summer, the analyst said. items.summary: The Houston Ship Channel and adjacent refineries, part of the Port of Houston, are seen in Houston, Texas, U.S., May 5, 2019. REUTERS/Loren Elliott Nov 6 (Reuters) – The Iran conflict has sent tanker rates soaring, forcing sellers to deepen discounts on heavy crude grades and giving US Gulf Coast refiners a cost advantage over Asian rivals, executives said after reporting bumper third-quarter profits. The disruption particularly benefited US Gulf Coast refiners, which could buy discounted heavy crude produced closer to home, including from Canada and Venezuela, while Asian rivals faced sharply higher freight and insurance costs to import similar grades through longer and riskiershipping routes. Rising freight costs have widened discounts on Canadian heavy crude, including Western Canadian Select (WCS), which typically trades below US benchmark West Texas Intermediate (WTI), creating a windfall for Gulf Coast refiners, as more than 70% of their facilities are configured to process heavier crude. Freight costs for shipping crude from the US Gulf Coast to Asia have jumped to $30-$35 a barrel from about $5 a year earlier, Hawkins said. “Higher freight rates actually give us an advantage into the typical export markets into Latin America,” said Gary Simmons, chief operating officer of Valero, adding that it mainly competes with European barrels in that market.

By comparison, only 25 ports were actively offering methanol bunkering. Those investing in ammonia- and hydrogen-capable ships face a far less mature infrastructure landscape. Singapore began licensing methanol suppliers from January 2026, while Shanghai recorded a single biomethanol transfer of 8,016 tonnes in August 2026. The scale-up has been dramatic, with single methanol transfers increasing from 475 tonnes at Antwerp-Bruges in 2023 to 8,016 tonnes in Shanghai in 2026. But you need time to find the information, and collectively, they can create another problem: fragmentation, where the knowledge and experience of employees become the integration layer. People have to move between systems, connect the information themselves, remember what needs to happen next, make notes on the side, or copy and paste (or script) information into Excel to try to make sense of it. Imagine looking at a vessel, port, or company and having much of the information you need connected to it. That changes the workflow, broadens your understanding, and hopefully gives you more time to do business. ShipIntel allows users to create alerts for vessels, ports, and areas. Instead of rebuilding the same market picture every morning, teams can create the view they need and monitor changes.

Spot prices of mainstream products at Qingdao port fell by about 3 yuan/mt on average. Iron ore stocks at 35 major Chinese ports stood at 149.13 million mt as of 6 November, up 1.08 million mt week-on-week, according to SMM. Arrivals are expected to recover next week, and port stocks may build further. On the demand side, average daily port outbound volume at the 35 ports fell 55,000 mt week-on-week to 3.12 million mt. Hot metal output at steel mills declined, and outbound volumes weakened with it. Momentum from the earlier short-covering rebound has faded, and pressure from the port stock build remains, limiting upside for futures. items.title: Tanker Fleet Growth Threatens Freight Boom, Bullish Secondhand Markets: Analysts
items.original_title: Tanker Fleet Growth Threatens Freight Boom, Bullish Secondhand Markets: Analysts
items.summary: A wave of tanker deliveries is set to test whether geopolitical disruption and longer trading routes can continue supporting charter rates and ship values, according to S&P Global Energy CERA’s latest fleet outlook, after an extraordinary freight market rally pushed some secondhand ship values above newbuilding order prices. Taking newbuild order books and scrapping into account, CERA analysts forecast global tanker capacity will rise from 703.72 million deadweight tons at the end of 2025 to 743.56 million dwt in 2026, 778.35 million dwt in 2027 and 830.61 million dwt in 2028, before reaching 862.98 million dwt in 2029. That would represent cumulative growth of 22.6% over four years. “The critical issue is not whether supply will grow, it clearly will, but whether ton-mile demand, scrapping, sanctions-related inefficiencies and operational segmentation can absorb that growth without a material decline in utilization and freight rates.” Record rates Tanker rates across segments have risen to record levels following the outbreak of the US-Iran war at the end of February, boosted by increased ship requirements as Asian importers seek barrels from farther afield and Middle Eastern producers rely on ship-to-ship transfers to mitigate transit risks around the Strait of Hormuz. Product tanker deliveries are more front-loaded, with Aframax/Long Range 2 and Medium Range growth expected to moderate after 2026-2027.

items.title: Ethanol-Fuelled Vessels Enter Dry Bulk Orderbook As Owners Seek Fuel Flexibility
items.original_title: Ethanol-Fuelled Vessels Enter Dry Bulk Orderbook As Owners Seek Fuel Flexibility
items.summary: These questions have become more relevant. Although the first methanol/ethanol-capable dry bulk vessels entered the orderbook in 2023, they gained popularity from May 2026, and the number increased to 19 vessels by September. The wider trend is equally interesting. LNG accounted for most of the alternative-fuel vessels in the dry bulk orderbook four years ago. The 19 methanol/ethanol-capable vessels currently in the dry bulk orderbook are linked to Vale’s move towards fuel-flexible ore carriers, with multiple shipowners ordering these vessels against long-term employment with the miner. Major cargo owners could also influence this shift if they increasingly include fuel capability and emissions in chartering decisions as they seek to reduce their Scope 3 emissions. Conclusion Nineteen methanol/ethanol-capable vessels on the orderbook do not signal a rapid shift towards ethanol. Instead, it shows that some owners have started paying for flexibility while the industry still lacks clarity on future fuel economics and regulations. For dry bulk shipping, this could ultimately create greater differentiation within the fleet.

items.title: PRC Research Vessels Nearly Double Survey Time Around Taiwan in 2026
items.original_title: PRC Research Vessels Nearly Double Survey Time Around Taiwan in 2026
items.summary: From January 1, 2018 to October 9, 2026, Windward MIOC analysis of 52 PRC research vessels shows several distinct changes in where and how the fleet works. The northern South China Sea’s share of fleet working time (slow-speed survey and station work offshore) rose from 22% in 2019–21 to 41% in 2023–25. China Geological Survey and academic vessels account for 78% of the added time, mainly over offshore oil, gas and gas-hydrate areas. In 2026, Effort Moved Toward Taiwan Jan–Sep working time within 300 NM of Taiwan rose from 3,862 to 7,411 hours compared with the same period in 2025, roughly doubling on both the Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines side and the mainland side, while fleet working time overall stayed roughly flat. Near Japan’s southwestern islands, slow-speed working time rose about eightfold, and the vessels involved match Japan Coast Guard reports of unauthorized survey activity. Instead faster seabed mapping around Guam increased in 2024. Field Program or Sustained Reallocation: Too Early to Tell There is a roughly even chance the 2026 increase around Taiwan reflects a recurring spring and summer field program rather than a sustained reallocation of effort. Activity through the winter and in spring 2027 will help distinguish between the two.

items.original_title: North Korean cargo ships crowd Russia’s Nakhodka amid coal, arms suspicions
items.summary: Last month, North Korean cargo ships repeatedly went in and out of the Russian Far East’s Nakhodka port. Because many were spotted around coal terminals and sanctioned vessels were among them, suspicions are being raised that trades are taking place to conceal the origin of North Korean coal. According to U.S.-based North Korea–focused outlet NK News on the 5th (local time), MarineTraffic ship-tracking data showed at least 13 North Korean ships recorded 14 visits to Nakhodka in October. North Korean ship visits to Nakhodka tallied through early November this year totaled 20, 14 of which were concentrated in October. Of the 13 North Korean ships that sent position signals near Nakhodka last month, at least nine were around coal terminals. Experts offered several possibilities for why North Korean ships have been turning up one after another at Russia’s coal terminals. Another notable point is the larger size of North Korean ships calling at Nakhodka this year. Whereas small fishing boats and refrigerated carriers mainly visited last year, large cargo ships have markedly increased this year. This raises the possibility that as North Korea–Russia trade expands, larger ships have been deployed, as well as the possibility of weapons transport.

items.summary: A Maersk Line containership seen alongside other ships a Hong Kong Convention-approved ship recycling facility in Alang, India. Photo credit: Maersk A European Parliament committee has voted to oppose the approval of two Indian ship recycling yards, dealing a setback to shipping industry efforts to expand access to South Asia’s shipbreaking facilities. The Parliament’s Environment Committee voted Wednesday to object to the European Commission’s proposal to add Shree Ram Vessel Scrap and YSI Recyclers, both located in Alang-Sosiya, Gujarat, to the European List of approved ship recycling facilities. The two yards had received preliminary backing from the European Commission following inspections intended to determine whether they meet the requirements of the EU Ship Recycling Regulation. The associations argue that the facilities have invested heavily in infrastructure, worker safety and environmental management, and that rejecting yards found compliant through the Commission’s inspection process would undermine the credibility of the EU approval system. “The inclusion of the two Indian yards in the EU list is a long-awaited and very welcome step, which rewards investments made to meet EU standards,” ECSA Secretary General Sotiris Raptis said in an October 28 statement . More than 95% of global ship recycling takes place in Bangladesh, India, Pakistan and Turkey, according to the shipping associations.

(Credit: Arctia) Finland expects to operate at least as many icebreakers in the coming decades as it does today, despite rising temperatures and declining average ice coverage in the Baltic Sea. This is the conclusion of a new government-commissioned report that also highlights growing security requirements and changes in the commercial shipping fleet. The report warns that the gap between a vessel’s theoretical ice classification and its actual operational capability is becoming more pronounced, potentially increasing demand for icebreaker assistance even as average ice conditions become milder. The first priority is the 1970s-built Urho and Sisu , followed by Kontio and Otso in the 2030s and the multipurpose icebreakers Fennica and Nordica in the 2040s. Finland relies heavily on maritime transport, with more than 95% of its foreign trade in goods carried by sea. The report says reliable winter navigation is essential not only for industrial supply chains and security of supply but also for military mobility. The agencies propose further work on the legal and procurement arrangements by the end of 2026.

items.summary: The Asia-North America tradelane is facing the highest ocean freight disruption risk over the coming weeks. Reduced carrier capacity and growing difficulty securing bookings threaten shipment reliability, according to WiseTech Global. The company’s November Ocean Freight Risk Outlook, released today covering weeks 45-48, rates the Asia-North America and Asia-Europe trades as high-risk overall, with Europe-North America assessed as medium risk. It explains that on the transpacific, planned carrier capacity is expected to tighten in the second half of November, driven by reduced supply rather than stronger demand. Booking security risk is also expected to climb to 71% by week 48, well above its historical average of 41%, suggesting growing difficulty securing space on preferred sailings. The latest weekly performance was just 6.5% on time, while 39.1% of arrivals saw delays of eight days or more. Shipment transit time reliability also fell across both Asian tradelanes in October, reaching 21% on Asia-North America, down six percentage points month on month, and 35% on Asia-Europe, a five-point decline. However, on-time performance fell from 39.2% in September to 34.8% in October, while the latest weekly result dropped to 24.6%. Transit-time reliability also weakened, falling three percentage points to 46%.

items.title: Cargo crime in North America down in Q3, but losses are mounting
items.original_title: Cargo crime in North America down in Q3, but losses are mounting
items.summary: Organised criminal networks are increasingly exploiting identity fraud, carrier impersonation and weaknesses in freight verification, driving cargo theft losses across Canada and the US up 39% year on year, despite a sharp decline in reported incidents Verisk CargoNet recorded 2,072 of reported supply chain crime incidents across the countries through to 23 October, marking a 25% decrease in total numbers from the 2,755 recorded during the comparable period in 2025. VP operations at Verisk CargoNet Keith Lewis told The Loadstar : “But while the number of incidents declined, the financial impact moved in the opposite direction, losses increasing 39% to $718.9m.” Furthermore, he noted that the average documented value of stolen goods had also registered a massive surge, 72% year on year, from approximately $261,000 to more than $448,000. Over the third quarter, CargoNet recorded 547 incidents, approximately 33% fewer than a year earlier, but estimated losses still reached $230.1m, with California accounting for the largest share, with 182 incidents, followed by New Jersey, Texas, and Illinois. Among the biggest concerns are fictitious pickups, where criminals impersonate legitimate carriers to collect and divert shipments, with CargoNet recording 138 such incidents in Q3, compared with 147 over the same period of 2025.

items.summary: Hong Kong is reviewing permit fees charged to river trade vessels as it seeks to maintain its port’s competitiveness amid growing competition from mainland Chinese terminals in Guangzhou and Shenzhen. The secretary for transport and logistics, Chan Mei-po, announced the review in a written reply to the Legislative Council on Wednesday. China-flagged vessels carry containers between ports in the Pearl River Delta and Hong Kong, where cargo may be transferred to ocean-going vessels for onward shipment. Hong Kong operates a multiple-entry permit scheme, allowing operators to make up to 10 port entries within a month for a fee equivalent to five single-entries – the “buy five, get five free” system. Ms Chan said: “The Action Plan on Maritime and Port Development Strategy proposes various measures to strengthen Hong Kong’s position as a regional transhipment hub, including reviewing the permit fees charged to river trade vessels in order to maintain the competitiveness and attractiveness of the port to the industry. We have completed a preliminary review and are now discussing the matter with relevant departments, with the details to be released in due course.” Laden container movements between Hong Kong and mainland China account for more than 40% of the territory’s annual laden container throughput.

items.summary: Thailand’s Precious Shipping is preparing a change at the top, with longtime managing director Khalid Moinuddin Hashim moving to executive vice chairman and finance chief Gautam Khurana taking over the running of the Bangkok-listed dry bulk owner. The company’s board approved the leadership reshuffle, with both appointments taking effect on January 1, 2027, according to a filing with the Stock Exchange of Thailand. Khurana will continue to serve as director of finance until a successor is appointed. The transition marks a significant shift for Precious Shipping, which has been led by Hashim for more than three decades. The management shake-up comes amid a major fleet renewal programme that has seen Precious sell ageing handysize and supramax vessels while expanding its ultramax fleet. In September, the company returned to China’s Taizhou Sanfu Ship Engineering for four 64,500 dwt ultramax newbuildings worth a combined $141.8m, with deliveries scheduled between April 2030 and January 2031. The order followed an earlier $133.46m contract for four 63,500 dwt ultramaxes at the same yard, with two vessels already in service and the remaining pair due through the first quarter of 2027. Once the outstanding newbuildings arrive, Precious expects its fleet to reach 47 vessels totalling about 2.34m dwt.

items.summary: The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA), the Research Council of Norway (RCN) and the Singapore Maritime Institute (SMI) have launched a joint research grant call to develop solutions to support the decarbonisation of international shipping. The joint grant call brings together the research, technology and industry capabilities of Singapore’s and Norway’s maritime innovation ecosystems to address shared technological and operational challenges and develop solutions applicable across international shipping. The grant call builds on the MPA-RCN Memorandum of Understanding signed in April 2024 on maritime research, development, education and training. The grant call will focus on three areas: · Alternative fuels and energy infrastructure: Improving the safety and handling of alternative marine fuels, developing bunkering and fuel storage technologies, and advancing charging infrastructure for electric vessels. · Digitalisation and greener shipping operations: Advancing voyage optimisation, just-in-time arrivals, autonomous operations and ship-port data exchange to improve operational efficiency and reduce emissions. SMI will provide up to S$2.7 million for Singapore research partners, while RCN will make available up to NOK 20 million for Norwegian research partners. Each proposal must involve research institutions and industry partners from both countries to ensure that the research addresses practical industry needs.

items.original_title: Kalé Research Identifies That Only Five Per Cent Of Ports Are Fully Digitised
items.summary: Only five percent of respondents said a Port Community System (PCS) was fully implemented at their port, according to new global research from Kalé Logistics (Kalé). Launched at the International Association of Ports and Harbors World Ports Conference, the State of Port Digital Readiness & Stakeholder Adoption of Port Community Systems report found half of respondents identified customs as the primary barrier to adoption, while 35 per cent cited other government agencies. “Ports are facing greater supply chain disruption, congestion, labour volatility, and compliance demands, but technology alone cannot solve these pressures while information remains fragmented between organisations and regulatory systems,” said Vineet Malhotra, Co-Founder and Director, Kalé. “The next phase of port digitalisation requires policy, people, and technology to move together, with authorities enabling trusted data exchange and ensuring developing markets are not left behind.” PCS connect public and private organisations across a port through a shared digital environment, allowing data to be securely exchanged and reused to reduce paperwork, congestion, delays, and duplicated processes, while improving cargo visibility and coordination. It finds 79 per cent of respondents report that their port does not have a fully operational PCS, while 22 per cent highlighted digital skills gaps as a barrier to adoption, and uptake remains particularly weak in low-income countries.

items.title: Advancing maritime digitalization in West and Central Africa
items.original_title: Advancing maritime digitalization in West and Central Africa
items.summary: The digitalization of ports across nine West and Central African countries has been boosted through a regional workshop in Accra, Ghana. The event was organized by IMO, the Africa Transport Policy Program (SSATP), and the World Bank, in partnership with the Ghana Maritime Authority. The key aims of the event included: • Promoting the adoption of the IMO Compendium on Facilitation and Electronic Business, which sets out how shipping and port data are structured and shared electronically to streamline communication; and • Scaling up the implementation of Maritime Single Windows (MSWs) and Port Community Systems (PCSs), which are integrated digital platforms that streamline vessel and cargo clearance, reduce bureaucratic delays, and will help to strengthen Africa’s competitiveness in global maritime trade. Promoting regional collaboration The workshop convened regional and international institutions committed to translating policy into action, including the Port Management Association of West and Central Africa (PMAWCA), the African Development Bank (AfDB), the African Harbour Masters’ Committee (AHMC), and the African Alliance for Electronic Commerce (AAEC). The workshop was structured around both knowledge sharing and practical capacity building, with 55 participants, including 15 women, from maritime administrations, port authorities, and customs authorities in Cabo Verde, Equatorial Guinea, The Gambia, Ghana, Guinea-Bissau, Liberia, Nigeria, São Tomé and Príncipe, and Sierra Leone.

items.title: Alfa Laval makes $700m NAVTOR bet
items.original_title: Alfa Laval makes $700m NAVTOR bet
items.summary: Swedish industrial group Alfa Laval has struck a $700m all-cash deal to acquire Norwegian maritime software specialist NAVTOR, significantly expanding a digital shipping portfolio that already includes StormGeo and Portchain. The Stockholm-listed group has entered into a definitive agreement to buy NAVTOR for SEK6.85bn ($700m), with completion expected during the first quarter of 2027 subject to regulatory approvals. Alfa Laval described the purchase as one of the most significant transactions in its history. Alfa Laval said it expects the business to generate about $194m in revenue this year. “With this acquisition, Alfa Laval will expand its digital offering at a time when real-time decision-making is increasingly complex,” said chief executive Tom Erixon. US technology investor Accel-KKR took a majority stake in NAVTOR in 2020, followed by purchases of performance analytics specialist Tres Solutions in 2021 and digital logbook developer Ingenium Marine in 2022. NAVTOR then combined with Voyager Worldwide in 2023, creating a business whose technology at the time served about 18,000 vessels. Alfa Laval has been assembling its own maritime software stack since buying weather routing and voyage optimisation company StormGeo for NOK3.63bn in 2021. Alfa Laval also disclosed that a recent NAVTOR internal review identified unspecified compliance matters, prompting the Norwegian company to strengthen its internal controls and compliance programme.
