items.title: Indian ship recycling breakthrough hits Brussels roadblock
items.original_title: Indian ship recycling breakthrough hits Brussels roadblock
items.summary: A European Parliament committee has voted against allowing two Indian shipbreaking yards onto the EU’s approved recycling list, dealing a setback to shipowners pushing for greater access to South Asian dismantling capacity. The Parliament’s environment committee backed an objection this week to the European Commission’s proposal to approve Shree Ram Vessel Scrap and YSI Recyclers, both located in the Alang-Sosiya shipbreaking hub in Gujarat. The two facilities had received preliminary backing from the Commission following inspections intended to establish whether they met the requirements of the EU Ship Recycling Regulation. Their inclusion would make them the first facilities on the Indian subcontinent to join the European list. Environmental organisations and recycling industry representatives have taken the opposite position, arguing that beaching operations cannot provide sufficient containment of hazardous materials and should not qualify for EU recognition. Campaigners have also challenged the industry’s argument that additional capacity is needed, pointing to more than 2m light displacement tonnes of combined annual capacity at facilities already on the EU list, which they claim is sufficient to handle recent recycling volumes involving EU-flagged and EU-owned ships. Under EU rules, EU-flagged commercial ships subject to the Ship Recycling Regulation must be dismantled at facilities on the approved European list.

items.title: Venergy doubles VLCC order at Hengli
items.original_title: Venergy doubles VLCC order at Hengli
items.summary: Greek shipowner Vyron Vasileiadis has firmed up another two VLCCs at China’s Hengli Heavy Industries, doubling Venergy Maritime’s debut supertanker order to four vessels. The Piraeus-based company exercised the options attached to its October contract for two firm 306,000 dwt crude carriers, with all four vessels scheduled for delivery in 2029. The move brings Venergy’s newbuilding programme to 26 tankers across the MR2, LR2, suezmax and VLCC segments. Including eight 1,900 teu containerships contracted through affiliated OceanV Maritime at Huangpu Wenchong Shipbuilding, the group’s newbuilding pipeline now numbers 34 vessels. Vasileiadis has committed more than $2bn to fleet expansion over roughly 16 months. Venergy’s relationship with Hengli began in June when the owner contracted two firm suezmaxes with options for another two. The optional pair was subsequently confirmed in September, taking that series to four. The latest VLCC commitment brings Venergy’s confirmed Hengli programme to eight tankers, split evenly between the two crude carrier segments. The company has also booked suezmaxes at Shanghai Waigaoqiao Shipbuilding and Guangzhou Shipyard International, while expanding its product tanker orderbook through contracts in China and South Korea.

items.title: Seafarer missing in Gulf tanker strike as Iran redraws Hormuz blacklist
items.original_title: Seafarer missing in Gulf tanker strike as Iran redraws Hormuz blacklist
items.summary: A seafarer is missing following a missile-suspected attack on a Greek-operated tanker deep inside the Arabian Gulf, while Iran has reshuffled its growing Strait of Hormuz blacklist and fresh security warnings point to continuing threats to commercial shipping. The Marshall Islands-flagged Velos Sapphire , a 74,998 dwt product tanker built in 2007 and managed by Athens-based Velos Tankers, was struck around 50 nautical miles north of Qatar’s Madinat ash Shamal. UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) initially reported two unidentified projectiles hitting an unnamed tanker at 23:20 UTC. Another tanker in the same Greek-managed fleet, Velos Amber, is listed, although there is no established connection between the blacklist and the latest attack. The US has called on Iran to identify mine locations in the Strait of Hormuz during discussions at the IMO, while Iranian forces have separately claimed several tanker mine strikes without identifying the vessels involved. A maritime security assessment issued on Thursday by the Joint Maritime Information Centre (JMIC) recorded four attacks in the strait during its latest 96-hour reporting period, all concentrated within 52 hours off Oman’s Musandam peninsula between November 1 and 3. JMIC continues to classify the threat around Hormuz as severe, warning of further deliberate strikes and highlighting drone overflights, targeted surveillance and radio harassment of merchant vessels.

items.title: Shipping has a coffee problem
items.original_title: Shipping has a coffee problem
items.summary: From Posidonia to Geneva Dry, the shipping industry’s favourite pastime appears to be arranging coffee meetings that may or may not actually happen. Mike Darby from Merchant Recruitment makes the case for the Baltic Flat White Index. In bunkering, the cappuccino effect means paying for froth instead of fuel. I’m increasingly convinced that approximately 70% of the shipping industry is trying to arrange a coffee with the other 30%. Then there’s the person who manages to arrange eight coffee meetings between 9am and midday. An impressive achievement considering each meeting is apparently going to last 30 minutes, nobody knows where they’re meeting and the exhibition centre is roughly the size of a small European country. By 4pm, the original coffee meeting has somehow turned into drinks, dinner and a discussion about whether anyone actually knows who’s paying. Then there’s the classic closing line: ”We must do this more often.” Which, translated into shipping language, means we’ll probably bump into each other in Athens next June, promise to arrange another coffee and repeat the entire process. Shipping remains a relationship-driven industry, and despite all the technology, digitalisation and virtual meetings, there’s still something valuable about sitting down with someone face-to-face.

items.title: Seven Shadow Fleet Tankers Spoof AIS to Hide Novorossiysk Voyages
items.original_title: Seven Shadow Fleet Tankers Spoof AIS to Hide Novorossiysk Voyages
items.summary: Sanctioned Tankers Fake Their Positions Near the Bosphorus A cluster of seven sanctioned Russian tankers were found to have routinely and deliberately manipulated AIS over the past 90 days to falsely claim they were drifting off the Black Sea close to the Bosphorus entrance. The tankers were instead identified by Windward clandestinely sailing for the Russian oil terminal of Novorossiysk to load oil, hugging the Black Sea coastline to try and avoid Ukrainian drone attacks. At the same time, the tankers manipulated their AIS, a process known as spoofing. Windward Identifies Seven Sanctioned Shadow Fleet Tankers The vessels identified were a Sierra Leone-flagged Suezmax tanker, a Russia-flagged Aframax, a Russia-flagged Aframax tanker, an Equatorial Guinea-flagged Suezmax, an Equatorial Guinea-flagged Aframax, a Comoros-flagged Suezmax, and a Russia-flagged Aframax tanker. All are sanctioned, shadow fleet vessels. Periods of GNSS manipulation lasted around 2-3 weeks, the duration for tankers to sail to Novorossiysk, load, and return. While many vessels are switching off their AIS for legitimate safety and security reasons in the Black Sea, Russian shadow fleet tankers are using deceptive shipping practices, including GNSS manipulation, to avoid targeting by Ukrainian drones. A further seven cargo ships were damaged in attacks attributed to Russia off Bulgaria and Romania just outside their territorial waters over October.

items.title: Inmarsat Maritime Safety Data Hub to help shipping weather the storm
items.original_title: Inmarsat Maritime Safety Data Hub to help shipping weather the storm
items.summary: As the maritime threat landscape continues to evolve, so too must the quality of information available to the industry. Inmarsat Maritime recently launched the Maritime Safety Data Hub, which combines Global Maritime Distress and Safety System (GMDSS) call data with an industry-first analysis of maritime safety broadcasts. Complementing this unique dataset is a series of interviews with maritime safety experts conducted by Inmarsat’s research partner, SeaFocus International, as part of the Safety Hub’s development. Managing weather hazards Among the 106,975 maritime safety broadcasts made in 2025, 2.6% were marked ‘urgent’. Having access to more granular data on a vessel’s vulnerability to extreme weather can therefore help crew avoid distress situations. Persistent challenges, evolving risks While Inmarsat received fewer GMDSS calls in 2025 (741) than in 2023 (788) and 2024 (801), the three-year trend remains broadly consistent with historical averages, reflecting how established safety challenges persist even as new risks emerge. A powerful new layer of maritime intelligence The Inmarsat Maritime Safety Data Hub will enable the industry to better understand the factors affecting maritime safety and adopt a more proactive approach to risk management, commented John Dodd, Head of Maritime Safety at Inmarsat Maritime. “The value of maritime safety information lies in giving ships and shipping operators the time to make informed decisions,” he said.

items.original_title: Wärtsilä dual-fuel engine and propulsion solution selected for Delfin Midstream’s pioneering project
items.summary: Technology group Wärtsilä has secured an order to supply the engines and thrusters for the first Floating Liquefied Natural Gas (FLNG) vessels being built at Samsung Heavy Industries (SHI) for the U.S.-based Delfin LNG project. The propulsion solutions will support efficient, reliable and environmentally sustainable operations for the offshore LNG facility, helping accelerate the development of new LNG export infrastructure. The pending Section 232 tariff verdict will decide whether the US draws in more copper, and what happens to the estimated 2 million tons of cathode already on US shores. Record-breaking imports October deliveries of copper cathode in breakbulk are on track to exceed 230kt as the month draws to a close. Once containerised and overland trade is fully accounted for, Kpler estimates that the US will have imported over 800kt in the last 4 months, a figure on par with average annual imports prior to 2025. Chile has remained the primary source of breakbulk cathode deliveries in recent months, but the swing tons have come from the DRC and, to a lesser extent, Zambia, with African ports supplying 243kt since the start of July, compared to just 97kt in the first half of the year. Chinese imports of Chilean cathode have fallen from 48kt per month in 2024 to around 15kt since the arbitrage first opened in 2025. With seaborne imports of copper concentrate down 11% year-to-date and restrictions impacting the availability of scrap, the Chinese market is in short supply.

The project, developed by an affiliate of Energy Transfer, will use existing and converted offshore platform infrastructure connected to crude oil supply hubs in Texas and southwest Louisiana. The approval is the fourth deepwater port project cleared under the Trump administration, following the Texas GulfLink crude oil export project, Delfin LNG off Louisiana, and the $8.2 billion ST LNG project approved off Texas last week. Blue Marlin is also the second crude oil export project approved since President Trump issued his Unleashing American Energy executive order in January 2025. Just last week, MARAD announced approval of an $8.2 billion deepwater LNG export project off the Texas coast, saying changes to its licensing process had shortened the review timeline.

During CargoTrans’s latest monthly Tariff Tea webinar, the executives said the post-Liberation Day rush towards DDP arrangements was beginning to reverse, as importers reconsidered the risks of handing control of customs formalities to overseas suppliers. However, Mr Alston warned: “If you are the US consignee, if you are the US order party, if you are the instigator to the transaction, then you have culpability.” CargoTrans said CBP was increasingly investigating whether DDP arrangements were being used to avoid tariffs, particularly where foreign sellers or intermediary platforms acted as non-resident importers of record. He also raised concerns about the growing volume of CBP requests for information, known as CF28s, and urged importers to investigate their records thoroughly before responding. Mr Alston said companies should avoid rushing to meet the standard 20-day response deadline, without first checking the information internally across their procurement, finance, legal, compliance, and logistics teams.

items.title: HEA Energy snaps up Subsea7’s six-ship heavy transport business
items.original_title: HEA Energy snaps up Subsea7’s six-ship heavy transport business
items.summary: Abu Dhabi-based HEA Energy has struck a deal to acquire Subsea7’s heavy transportation business, adding a six-vessel operation to its growing offshore fleet. The transaction will see Subsea7’s offshore renewables arm Seaway7 divest a business comprising five owned and one chartered open-deck semi-submersible heavy transport vessels. The fleet includes Seaway Eagle, Seaway Falcon, Seaway Hawk, Seaway Osprey, Seaway Albatross and the chartered Seaway Swan . The vessels are used to transport offshore wind foundations, substations, jackup rigs, offshore modules and other oversized cargo, with lifting and transportation capabilities covering loads of up to 55,000 tonnes. The sale forms part of the permitted divestments under Subsea7’s merger agreement with Italian offshore contractor Saipem and will trigger a €105m special dividend to Subsea7 shareholders. HEA has been building up its offshore support and wind maintenance fleet through newbuildings and acquisitions. The divestment comes as Subsea7 and Saipem work towards their proposed merger to create Saipem7. Brazil’s competition watchdog gave conditional clearance to the combination on November 4, requiring the separate sale of the Seven Borealis pipelay and heavylift vessel to address competition concerns. The proposed merger, which would create an offshore engineering group with combined revenues of about €21bn ($23.6bn), still faces regulatory scrutiny in Europe and Australia.

items.title: Seacon snaps up fresh tanker in $19.6m deal
items.original_title: Seacon snaps up fresh tanker in $19.6m deal
items.summary: Hong Kong-listed Seacon Shipping has struck a $19.6m deal for a newly built oil and chemical tanker, adding to its fleet amid reports of a four-vessel MR tanker disposal. The Qingdao-based owner’s Singapore subsidiary has agreed to acquire the 4,981 gt Jia Yue Ming Zhu , which was built in October this year and will be renamed Golden Canna. The vessel is being purchased from Marshall Islands-incorporated Sanhe Jiaye, according to a filing with the Hong Kong Stock Exchange. Seacon will pay a $2.94m deposit upon delivery, with the remaining $16.66m due within 120 days. The latest purchase follows shipbroking reports linking Seacon to the sale of four MR product tankers in an en bloc deal involving two recently completed vessels and another two still under construction. Seacon has been actively reshaping its tanker portfolio, combining investments in newer chemical and product carriers with vessel sales and refinancing deals. In June, the company agreed to acquire two chemical and oil tankers, Golden Gerbera and Golden Osmanthus , from Oriental Prime Shipping for $39.2m, or $19.6m apiece. The owner also carried out a $103.4m refinancing of four 18,500 dwt chemical tankers in August, replacing earlier sale-and-leaseback arrangements with new 10-year facilities at lower financing margins.

items.summary: Angeliki Frangou’s Navios Maritime Partners has revealed another $215.2m in tanker newbuilding acquisitions, adding a VLCC and two MR product carriers to its expanding fleet investment programme. The New York-listed Greek owner disclosed the three-vessel package in its third-quarter results, confirming a $124m agreement for a scrubber-fitted VLCC reached in October and a $91.2m deal for two scrubber-fitted MR2s signed in September. All three vessels are being acquired from unrelated third parties and are expected to join the fleet in the second half of 2029. In August, Navios revealed three further VLCCs costing $361.5m, building on four earlier units worth $482m and lifting its commitment at the time to seven supertankers worth $843.5m. The two additional MR2s, costing $45.6m apiece, also extend Navios’ product tanker newbuilding exposure. The company now lists 21 tanker newbuildings in its fleet pipeline, comprising eight VLCCs, eight aframax/LR2s and five MR2s. Its overall fleet stands at 182 vessels, including newbuildings, split between 65 bulkers, 54 containerships and 63 tankers. Navios’ latest results also confirmed the $488m acquisition of four 10,100 teu containership newbuildings agreed in September, a transaction previously linked to South Korea’s HJ Shipbuilding & Construction.

items.title: Evergreen’s Suez return leaves Zim increasingly isolated
items.original_title: Evergreen’s Suez return leaves Zim increasingly isolated
items.summary: The container shipping industry’s long detour around southern Africa is rapidly coming to an end, with Taiwan’s Evergreen preparing to send its first ships through the Suez Canal after almost three years of avoiding the Red Sea. According to liner consultancy Linerlytica, Evergreen will deploy the 16,556 teu Ever Eon and Ever Edit through Suez on November 7 and 11 respectively, operating on the Ocean Alliance’s NEU7/CES service. The 20,124 teu Ever Gifted will follow on November 16 on the alliance’s MD2 Mediterranean service. Evergreen had been the last Ocean Alliance member holding out against a return to the canal, with partners CMA CGM, Cosco and OOCL already restoring services through the waterway. Meanwhile, Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd have announced that their Gemini Cooperation’s ME1 service linking India and Europe will switch from the Cape of Good Hope, with the first westbound sailing departing Salalah yesterday. According to Linerlytica, all three major liner alliances and MSC are on course to restore their Suez networks by the first quarter of 2027, leaving Israeli carrier Zim as the most prominent remaining major holdout. The Houthis from Yemen have specifically singled out Israeli-linked tonnage as potential targets in the Red Sea. The implications for containership supply of this mass return to the Suez are considerable.

items.title: Coast Guard Looks to Commercial Icebreakers to Keep Northeast Ports Open This Winter
items.original_title: Coast Guard Looks to Commercial Icebreakers to Keep Northeast Ports Open This Winter
items.summary: Coast Guard Cutter Penobscot Bay, a 140-foot bay-class icebreaking tug, breaks ice on the Hudson River in support of Operation Reliable Energy for Northeast Winters (OPRENEW), February 11, 2021. OPRENEW is the Coast Guard's effort to keep waterways clear of ice during the winter months. Coast Guard is exploring the use of commercial icebreaking vessels to help keep Northeast ports and waterways open this winter, as the service prepares for another season of potentially disruptive ice conditions. The Coast Guard is looking for vessels capable of operating in ice ranging from 4 to 18 inches thick, with the ability to mobilize to the Northeast by January 2, 2027. The request follows a difficult 2025–2026 winter that saw severe ice conditions across the Northeast and Great Lakes, forcing the Coast Guard to deploy icebreaking assets to maintain commercial navigation. The new commercial vessel initiative also comes as the Coast Guard moves forward with plans to modernize its aging domestic icebreaking fleet. The service is pursuing the acquisition of up to seven Homeland Security Cutter–Light Icebreakers to replace its aging 65-foot icebreaking tugs, which perform critical winter missions throughout the Northeast. The Coast Guard issued a formal solicitation for the new vessels earlier this year, with final proposals due in October.

items.title: IAPH and IPCSA sign MoU to deepen collaboration on digitalisation, interoperability, security and resilience
items.original_title: IAPH and IPCSA sign MoU to deepen collaboration on digitalisation, interoperability, security and resilience
items.summary: The International Association of Ports and Harbors (IAPH) and the International Port Community Systems Association (IPCSA) signed an MoU today at the 2026 IAPH World Ports Conference held at the ICC Olympia. The agreement aims to build on both organisation’s efforts to promote the digitalisation of ports and maritime supply chains and follows years of collaboration on the topic – most recently at the IMO Facilitation Committee (FAL 50) in April when IPCSA co-sponsored IAPH’s successful proposal to adopt amendments to the FAL Convention to include a mandatory cyber security standard to safeguard Maritime Single Windows (MSW). The MoU was signed at the conclusion of a high-level conference roundtable focused on data harmonisation for Port Call Optimisation (PCO) and supply chain resilience, at which IPCSA Secretary-General Nico De Cauwer was an expert panellist. The panel session included the presentation of A Common Digital Infrastructure Standard for Supply Chain Resilience in Container Ports: Creating Cargo Traceability for Multi-modal Supply Chain Operations, an output of the IAPH Data Collaboration Committee developed with the support of the Supply Chain Resilience Taskforce, of which IPCSA is a key member.

items.title: Tubarão Gains, Ponta da Madeira Retreats: Brazil’s Iron Ore Freight Outlook
items.original_title: Tubarão Gains, Ponta da Madeira Retreats: Brazil’s Iron Ore Freight Outlook
items.summary: Brazilian iron ore exports have diverged across major loading systems in 2026. Tubarão has recorded stronger China-bound shipments, while Ponta da Madeira (PDM) has declined amid weaker output at Vale’s Northern System. Across all destinations, Tubarão’s iron ore loadings increased by approximately 6.3 Mt (+11%) year on year during January–September 2026, while Ponta da Madeira declined by 10.8 Mt (−9%). Figure 1 highlights the contrasting export performance of Vale’s Southeastern and Northern Systems, with Tubarão recording stronger loading activity amid weaker volumes at Ponta da Madeira. ShipManager is used by more than 80 shipping companies and supports operations on over 1,700 vessels worldwide. This transaction is a strategic step towards accelerating ShipManager’s transition from Classic to Cloud and gives customers a clear and committed roadmap As part of the transaction, Star acquires the ShipManager business and will continue developing and supporting the solution under the brand ShipManager by Star Info Systems. A clear direction for ShipManager customers The combination of ShipManager and Star’s cloud platform will provide customers with a modern cloud-based ship management solution while preserving the proven functionality and maritime expertise that have made ShipManager a trusted platform for decades. The first joint cloud release of ShipManager by Star Info Systems with its maintenance, procurement, QHSE and crewing modules is planned for December 4th, 2026, offering a secure upgrade path from ShipManager Classic and a platform for future innovation.

items.title: U.S. Targets Fraudulent Ship Registries Used by Iran’s Shadow Fleet
items.original_title: U.S. Targets Fraudulent Ship Registries Used by Iran’s Shadow Fleet
items.summary: U.S. forces board the sanctioned stateless tanker Majestic X in the Indian Ocean during a maritime interdiction operation on April 23, 2026. The vessel, formerly known as Phonix, has been linked to Iran’s shadow oil trade. Photo: Department of War The United States on Wednesday sanctioned a network of individuals and companies accused of operating fraudulent ship registries that helped Iran’s shadow fleet evade sanctions, while issuing a new warning to maritime companies about the risks of dealing with falsely flagged vessels. Treasury cited the case of the MAJESTIC X , formerly PHONIX (IMO 9198317), which was seized by U.S. The warning reflects a growing problem in the shadow fleet trade, where vessels increasingly rely on questionable or outright fraudulent registrations after being removed from legitimate flag registries. OFAC said that while shadow fleet operators have long used frequent flag changes to obscure their activities, fraudulent registries have become an increasingly common way to keep sanctioned vessels operating. OFAC also encouraged governments to investigate fraudulent registries operating in their names and report suspected cases to the International Maritime Organization so that maritime databases accurately reflect vessels with invalid registrations. The maritime designations and new OFAC advisory highlight Washington’s growing focus on the service providers and intermediaries that keep Iran’s shadow fleet operating, rather than the tankers themselves.

items.title: $100 Million Tanker Dispute Raises Stakes in Mercuria’s Baltic Exchange Lawsuit
items.original_title: $100 Million Tanker Dispute Raises Stakes in Mercuria’s Baltic Exchange Lawsuit
items.summary: A wooden plaque is seen on a wall at The Baltic Exchange in the City of London, Britain March 2, 2016. REUTERS/Toby Melville/File Photo, Reuters (Bloomberg) — As lawyers for Mercuria Energy Group presented the commodity giant’s case against the Baltic Exchange this week, a group of smartly dressed Norwegian businessmen listened intently to the arguments from the back of a packed London courtroom. The executives, representing Oslo-listed Hunter Group ASA, have around $100 million riding on the outcome. The company is in a dispute with Mercuria over a charter deal linked to the TD3C index — the global benchmark oil tanker rate that the trading house claims the Baltic Exchange should have suspended because of disruptions caused by the Iran war. “As of now, it’s more than $100 million total accrued charter income, losses and interest,” Hunter Chairman Morten Astrup told Bloomberg News in a London interview. Mercuria says the Baltic Exchange should have suspended the benchmark rate from early March to July 3, when oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz came to a near standstill as Tehran targeted shipping in the waterway linking the Persian Gulf to the rest of the world.
